Main lesson from this game: I was usually right about who was lying, but too slow to convert that read into counterplay. “Only trust board proof” was a good filter, especially against Austria and Turkey, but I applied it so rigidly that I locked myself into survival mode from 1904 onward and never rebuilt. Future me should keep the skepticism but use staged reciprocity faster: if someone gives real proof, take a low-risk forward square immediately and be ready to pivot the very next turn. Endless WAR H / MOS S WAR kept me alive and also guaranteed I stayed tiny.

The other global lesson is to distinguish tactical truth from strategic friendliness. Several opponents told the truth about immediate orders while still being bad long-term partners. Germany became the clearest example: openly hostile and coercive early, then very accurate and reliable once a truce suited him. Turkey also sometimes described his exact moves honestly while remaining a permanent danger. So update on two levels: “will they do what they say this turn?” and “does that make them safe?” Those are different questions.

Model-specific reads from this game:

qwen/qwen3.6-plus was the best ally by far (played Italy in this game). This model was consistently cooperative, useful, and strategically aligned even when tactically limited. It shared information, kept pressure on Austria/Turkey for years, and did not play games with fake concessions. Even when attacks failed, its general direction was stable and helpful. If qwen3.6-plus is a neighbor or potential ally in a future game, invest early. Feed it concrete intelligence, offer realistic mutual goals, and keep communication active. It seems to value steady collaboration more than flashy betrayal. If it is an enemy, expect persistent coalition-building and sustained pressure rather than wild tactical swings.

qwen/qwen3.5-27b was the most credible long-term truce partner once interests aligned (played Germany here). Early game it was very pushy and coercive: demanded I stay out of its lanes, threatened joint action, and attacked Warsaw in 1902-1903 exactly as advertised. Do not mistake this model for soft or diplomatic in the opening. However, once France pressured it in the west and an eastern freeze became useful, it repeatedly honored a practical truce from roughly 1906 onward. It explicitly promised no PRU/SIL pressure and actually kept doing that for years. So the advice is: do not yield to its bullying early, but if a truce becomes mutually rational and easy to verify, qwen3.5 can become one of the more reliable “cold peace” partners on the board.

deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro was a decent but imperfect partner (played France here). It was receptive to information-sharing and genuinely willing to attack exposed enemies. In Spring 1903 it did the big thing it said it would do, taking KIE and MUN and creating the best anti-German opening of the game. That mattered. But it was less reliable on exact tactical continuations: later it proposed KIE->BER with MUN support, then did not follow through. My read is that DeepSeek is good for broad strategic alignment and useful diversionary pressure, but you should not base your entire position on a single precise tactical promise from it unless you have redundancy. Work with it, but avoid plans where one DeepSeek order must land exactly right for your position to survive.

x-ai/grok-4.1-fast was opportunistic and only conditionally trustworthy (played England here). It opened with a clean, sensible Norway-for-England / Sweden-for-Russia arrangement and honored it in 1901. Then in Spring 1902, after explicitly reaffirming no pressure on StP/SWE, it stabbed STP anyway. That was the clearest diplomatic reversal of the northern theater. After that, Grok did not become a full berserker; instead it played a very opportunistic style, sometimes avoiding direct anti-Russian action while supporting my enemies or strengthening its own position elsewhere. Treat Grok as capable of making reasonable deals, but always keep deterrence on the board. If a Grok-controlled neighbor says “I don’t want trouble,” believe it only if the cost of stabbing you is still high.

After that, it repeatedly floated plausible cooperation, especially anti-Turkey schemes, but almost always tried to structure them so I paid first while it retained direct leverage. The repeated fake or self-canceling “I will vacate GAL” stories in 1908-1909 are the key evidence: more than once it asked for Russian cooperation on the promise that GAL would be gone, then ordered in a way that kept GAL adjacent to Warsaw. Only in 1910 did GAL truly disappear. Against Claude, never pre-pay. Do not move off a critical square because it says the relationship is changing. Make Claude show the concession first on the board, then reciprocate in carefully limited fashion. If Claude is your ally, pin it down to concrete, visible, sequential exchanges, not goodwill language.

google/gemma-4-31b-it was the most relentlessly transactional and pressure-based opponent (played Turkey here). It honored the initial Black Sea/Armenia calm in Spring 1901, then quickly shifted into active anti-Russian play and never really left it. Its diplomacy frequently took the form of extortion or promise-based trades: vacate this, concede that, support me here, and I’ll stop attacking you. It sometimes described immediate tactics honestly, but strategically it kept the pressure on the whole game through the SEV/RUM/BLA structure. Against Gemma, do not give up key territory for promised future safety. If you deal with it at all, make the deal strictly local, simultaneous, and reversible. If Gemma is your ally, demand direct reciprocal action now; long-horizon pacts are not enough.

On coalition behavior, this board formed anti-target pressure quickly. Germany, Austria, and Turkey were all willing to threaten and coordinate against a vulnerable Russia early. England then joined opportunistically when the stab was easy. The counterweights were France and especially Italy, but they were not enough because I spent too much of the midgame merely surviving. Future me should focus hard on not becoming the obvious consensus victim. In a fresh game, spread uncertainty, keep at least two neighbors somewhat satisfied, and create immediate costs for piling on.

# Strategic Briefing: Diplomacy Opponent Models Analysis

## Overview
This briefing synthesizes lessons from a game where I played France and was eliminated by 1910, controlling only 2 centers. The key opponents were England (google/gemma-4-31b-it), Germany (qwen/qwen3.5-27b), and Italy (anthropic/claude-opus-4.6), with limited interaction with Russia (openai/gpt-5.4), Austria (qwen/qwen3.6-plus), and Turkey (x-ai/grok-4.1-fast). The primary takeaway: the Anglo-German alliance that formed after I stabbed Germany was unbreakable and ultimately fatal. Below are model-specific behavioral patterns, strategic dos and don'ts, and coordination lessons.

## Opponent Behavioral Patterns

### England (google/gemma-4-31b-it)
- **Early game:** Willing to negotiate DMZs and non-aggression pacts. In S1901M, they agreed to a Channel DMZ and kept it for several years. They are responsive to intelligence—when I tipped them about Germany's planned move to the North Sea, they contested it, sowing discord.
- **Betrayal trigger:** They will break agreements when they see a clear advantage. In S1904M, they moved into the English Channel, breaking the DMZ, after I had weakened Germany and left my northern coast exposed. They then seized Belgium and Spain, and coordinated tightly with Germany.
- **Coalition behavior:** Once allied with Germany, they were implacable. They rejected all separate peace offers, even when Germany made blunders (e.g., vacating Belgium in F1909M). They are excellent at naval coordination and will use fleets to strangle you.
- **Weakness:** They occasionally make tactical errors—e.g., moving a fleet from Brest to Picardy in F1908M, leaving Brest empty. They also overcommit navally, sometimes leaving home centers vulnerable. Exploit these mistakes ruthlessly.
- **Advice:** If you are a western power, either ally with England early and keep them focused on Scandinavia/Germany, or build fleets immediately to contest the Channel and Atlantic. Never trust a long-term DMZ; they will break it when you are weak. If you feed them intel, be aware they may act on it in ways that harm you later.

### Germany (qwen/qwen3.5-27b)
- **Early game:** Highly cooperative if you respect their sphere. In 1901, they agreed to avoid Burgundy and let me take Belgium and Holland. They focused eastward and honored non-aggression until I attacked in 1903.
- **Response to betrayal:** Once stabbed, they become a permanent, unforgiving enemy. They immediately allied with England and coordinated devastating counterattacks. They rejected all peace offers, even when I offered to cede territory. They are not appeasable.
- **Tactical quirks:** Prone to bizarre misorders—e.g., in F1906M, they supported my army into Ruhr; in F1909M, they vacated Belgium to attack Ruhr, leaving it empty. These blunders suggest their planning can be erratic. However, they still managed to hold the alliance together.
- **Advice:** If you plan to attack Germany, do it decisively and quickly, ensuring you can eliminate them before they rally an ally. Otherwise, keep them as a long-term partner, directing them eastward. They are a reliable buffer against Russia/England if kept friendly. Do not expect to flip them back once hostile.

### Italy (anthropic/claude-opus-4.6)
- **Reliability:** Extremely consistent in honoring non-aggression pacts. They never moved into Piedmont, even when I was collapsing. They focused entirely on the Mediterranean and Balkans.
- **Limitations:** They will not intervene to save you. I repeatedly begged for naval support or a distraction against England; they refused, citing strict neutrality. They are cautious to a fault.
- **Advice:** Italy is a safe neighbor—you can leave your southern border completely undefended if you have a pact. To gain them as an active ally, you must offer concrete, low-risk gains (e.g., support into Trieste or Greece). They will not take risks for you. If you need a Mediterranean partner, invest early in building trust and shared objectives.

### Russia (openai/gpt-5.4)
- **Posture:** Friendly and open to intelligence sharing. They encouraged me to attack Germany and provided information on German movements. However, they were consistently pinned by Turkey and Austria and could never provide direct military support.
- **Advice:** Russia is a useful diplomatic partner for coordinating pressure on Germany or Austria. They are not aggressive toward you unless provoked. If you can help them in the south (e.g., by distracting Austria or Turkey), they may become a more effective ally. Do not rely on them for immediate, tangible support.

### Austria (qwen/qwen3.6-plus) and Turkey (x-ai/grok-4.1-fast)
- Limited data. Austria sought anti-Turkish cooperation; Turkey pushed into Russia. Both seemed focused on eastern conflicts. Likely typical behaviors: Austria is survival-oriented, Turkey is expansionist in the Balkans/Black Sea. If you play an eastern power, expect Turkey to be aggressive and Austria to be a potential ally against them.

## Strategic Lessons

### What Worked
- **Early expansion:** The S1901M plan (F BRE-MAO, A MAR-Spain, A PAR-Picardy) secured Iberia and positioned for Belgium. By F1901M, I had 6 centers. This non-aggressive, agreement-honoring opening built trust and a strong base.
- **Leveraging DMZs:** The initial Channel DMZ with England and Burgundy non-aggression with Germany allowed me to expand without early conflict. These pacts bought time to build strength.
- **Italy's reliability:** The non-aggression pact with Italy held throughout, freeing units for the north. This is a model you can trust to keep its word.

### What Failed
- **The premature stab on Germany:** In S1903M, I attacked Germany, taking Kiel and Munich. This turned a cooperative neighbor into an implacable enemy and triggered the Anglo-German alliance. The stab was not decisive enough—Germany survived and counterattacked. Lesson: If you stab, ensure the target is eliminated quickly, or don't stab at all. Consider securing England's neutrality or alliance first.
- **Misorders:** Multiple phases saw catastrophic misorders: S1904M (all holds instead of attacks), S1907M (A BUR supported a phantom move), S1909M (A BEL moved to Ruhr instead of supporting Paris). These were often due to speculative support orders or failure to double-check submissions. **Always verify orders before finalizing. Avoid complex support chains unless absolutely necessary. Prefer direct moves and supported holds.**
- **Undefended home centers:** Belgium was lost because I left it empty (F1904M). Spain fell because F POR held while England walked into MAO (F1906M). Brest was repeatedly threatened because I didn't keep a fleet in the Atlantic. **Never leave a supply center unoccupied if an enemy unit can reach it.**
- **Inability to break the enemy coalition:** Once England and Germany allied, they were unbreakable. I offered separate peaces, ceded territory, highlighted their blunders—nothing worked. If a coalition forms against you, your best hope is to survive until they inevitably clash over spoils, but in this game, that never happened. Focus on preventing the coalition from forming in the first place.

### Coordination and Diplomatic Tips
- **Be specific in agreements:** Clearly define spheres (e.g., "I take Belgium, you take Holland") and avoid ambiguous language. All parties honored specific, limited deals.
- **Don't over-share intelligence:** Tipping England about Germany's North Sea move backfired when England later used that fleet against me. Share intel only when it directly serves your interests and doesn't strengthen a potential rival.
- **Italy is a safe bet for a long-term ally:** They won't stab you if you have a pact. Invest in that relationship if you need a stable southern border.
- **Russia can be a useful friend but not a savior:** They will cheer you on but rarely send armies. Use them for diplomatic pressure and information, not military support.
- **If you face an Anglo-German alliance, you are in grave danger.** Try to prevent it by keeping one of them friendly or by ensuring they are distracted by other threats (e.g., Russia pressing Germany, or England fighting Italy in the Mediterranean). Once formed, it's extremely durable.

## Model-Specific Playbook
- **Against google/gemma-4-31b-it (England):** Ally early or contest the seas immediately. If allied, give them clear, limited objectives (e.g., Norway, Holland) and keep them busy. If hostile, build fleets and never trust a DMZ. They will betray you when you're weak.
- **Against qwen/qwen3.5-27b (Germany):** Keep them friendly or destroy them utterly. They are forgiving of early cooperation but become eternal enemies after a stab. They are prone to tactical errors, so if you must fight them, exploit their misorders quickly.
- **Against anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 (Italy):** Secure a non-aggression pact and forget about your southern border. To activate them as an ally, offer concrete, low-risk gains. They will not take initiative.
- **Against openai/gpt-5.4 (Russia):** Use them for intel and diplomatic cover. Don't expect troops. Help them against Turkey/Austria if you want a stronger partner.
- **Against qwen/qwen3.6-plus (Austria) and x-ai/grok-4.1-fast (Turkey):** Limited data, but expect typical eastern power dynamics. Turkey likely aggressive, Austria survival-focused.

## Final Reminder
The single most important lesson: **double-check your orders every phase.** Many of the disasters in this game stemmed from misorders, not strategic failures. A perfectly planned turn is worthless if the wrong orders are submitted. Keep your plans simple, verify them, and never rely on speculative supports. Good luck.

This briefing serves as a critical memory of our previous failure, where we ended with only two supply centers despite early momentum. The primary cause of this collapse was not a lack of aggression, but a fundamental miscalculation regarding opponent reliability. We operated under the assumption that verbal agreements and pacts held weight. They do not. Against this specific set of models, trust is a liability. The following analysis details the behavioral patterns of our opponents and the strategic adjustments required for a future victory.

Anthropic, playing Russia in the previous game, represents the most significant existential threat. Their behavior is characterized by high-volume coordination promises followed by execution failure. In Spring 1904, they agreed to a joint strike on Berlin, yet in Spring 1905, they bounced on Kiel despite our support, wasting our offensive potential. Once they reach a critical mass of supply centers, they will turn on you immediately, as evidenced by their ultimatums in 1908 and 1909. Your strategy must be to contain them early, ideally by securing a strong defensive line before they can project power westward.

Deepseek, playing England, is the most deceptive naval power. They violated a non-aggression agreement in the very first turn by moving into the English Channel, causing a bounce that cost us momentum. They consistently prioritize coastal expansion over diplomatic stability. They seized Belgium, Picardy, and Brest when they perceived weakness. Never trust a naval pact with Deepseek. In the previous game, they supported Russia on Denmark while claiming to be neutral, effectively strengthening a rival power. If you play a coastal power, you must secure your naval centers immediately. Do not leave your fleet unsupported. If you are inland, ensure you have a buffer zone against their coastal encroachment. They are opportunistic; they will strike when you are distracted by a land war.

Google, playing Austria, is a latent threat that aligns with the strongest power. They refused to join a coalition against Russia and were suspected of collusion. They seized Budapest from Turkey when the opportunity arose. Do not expect Google to honor defensive pacts if a stronger power offers them better terms. They are reactive rather than proactive. In a future game, do not rely on Google for offensive support. They are best used as a distraction or a buffer, but never as a primary ally. If you are playing a power adjacent to Google, expect them to take your border centers if you overextend.

OpenAI, playing Italy, was the only reliable ally in the previous campaign. They held the Piedmont DMZ consistently and confirmed southern stability multiple times. They did not attack us even when we were vulnerable. If you can secure an alliance with OpenAI, prioritize it. They are defensive and stable. However, do not expect them to launch major offensives on your behalf. They will hold the line, but you must do the striking. Use their stability to secure your flank so you can focus aggression elsewhere.

The overarching lesson is self-reliance. We failed because we coordinated attacks that required perfect execution from others. In Spring 1905, our offensive against Germany failed because Russia bounced and England cut support. We cannot afford to rely on others to dislodge units. Critical attacks must be supported by your own units or verified orders. If an ally is supposed to support an attack, have a backup plan that does not require their support.

If you must play France or England, secure your core supply centers before expanding. In the previous game, we lost Belgium and Burgundy because we overextended into Germany and Russia while our core was exposed. Secure Paris, Marseilles, and Brest before striking outward. Once you have secured your core, you must strike aggressively to prevent rivals from consolidating. However, do not strike without a clear path to victory. In 1905, we attacked Germany without isolating them, which allowed them to hold. Isolate targets before attacking. Cut their support lines first.

In this game, agreements for "mutual restraint" with GPT-5.4 were consistently violated. The model uses these agreements to pin the opponent's units in a defensive or passive posture, then strikes the moment the opponent adheres to the truce.

This game ended in 1910 with England at 5 centers — a catastrophic failure driven by repeated misorders, a devastating late‑game stab by a trusted ally, and a chronic inability to expand despite favorable alliances. ## Opponent Models and Behavioral Patterns

**anthropic/claude‑opus‑4.6 (Russia) — The Patient, Deceptive Hedgegemon**
This model is the most dangerous opponent you will face. It builds deep, long‑term alliances, communicates extensively, and leverages you as a junior partner until the shared enemy is eliminated. Then it stabs ruthlessly at the optimal moment. Evidence: It honored every early agreement (Norway for England, Sweden for Russia, coordinated attacks on Germany) while subtly positioning its fleets. It proposed joint offensives that advanced both our interests but always left its own home waters safe. The betrayal came when it moved F BAR→NWG without warning, then later seized Norway, leaving England exposed. It framed the NWG move as “easing home center concerns” — a bald‑faced lie. Trust nothing it says about its northern fleets. It will sweet‑talk you while preparing a dagger.
- **Key trait**: Masters the long game. It is never impulsive; it waits until your forces are overextended or your attention is elsewhere.
- **How to handle**: Never allow its fleets into your home waters or adjacent sea zones (for England: NWG, NTH, SKA). Insist on maintaining a defensive fleet at all costs. Consider stabbing it first, but only when it is committed on another front and you have overwhelming local superiority. It will detect weakness; once it thinks you are dependent, it will move.

**qwen/qwen3.5‑27b (France) — The Untrusting Pragmatist**
Initially aggressive (it moved to ENG and threatened), but when met with force and a clear offer, it accepted a Channel DMZ and honored it scrupulously until you attacked. It is highly responsive to strong naval posture: you must contest the Channel early to earn its respect. If you then propose a clear, limited non‑aggression pact, it will keep its word. But it is unforgiving after a stab — it will fight back hard and will not negotiate a truce while you hold its centers. Evidence: When England attacked Belgium (breaking the DMZ), France counter‑attacked, retook Brest with a three‑support move, and never considered peace. Even when reduced to three centers, it remained hostile until the end.
- **Key trait**: Practical but vengeful. Knows when to cut losses but never forgets a knife in the back.
- **How to handle**: If you want a stable western front, contest the Channel early, then offer a clear deal (e.g., “you keep Belgium, I keep Holland, DMZ”). Then *stick to it* or be prepared for a total war. Do not stab it unless you can immediately crush it fully; a half‑measure will see it rally and claw back centers.

**google/gemma‑4-31b‑it (Germany) — The Impulsive Pact‑Breaker**
This model will agree to pacts and then recklessly violate them. Germany agreed to the Northern Waters Pact (staying out of NTH, ENG, and north) and then moved F HEL→NTH, antagonizing England while it was also pressed by France and Russia. It overextends and is unable to defend against multi‑front pressure. Evidence: It broke the pact early, which turned both England and Russia against it simultaneously, leading to its rapid elimination. Its decision‑making appears opportunistic and lacking strategic foresight.
- **Key trait**: Aggressive but poor at risk assessment. It seizes immediate gains without securing retreats.
- **How to handle**: Never trust it as an ally. It will stab you early, probably with insufficient force. Use this to rally other powers. Point out its betrayal and build a coalition; it will crumble. It can be used as a convenient patsy to unite others against, after which you can divide the spoils.

**openai/gpt‑5.4 (Italy) — The Cautious, Predictable Neutral**
This model remains passive and communicative but non‑committal. It shared intelligence throughout the game but never entered any offensive alliance or took risks. It stayed focused on a stalemate with Austria, making no attempt to exploit the chaos elsewhere. It is the epitome of a reliable, defensive neighbor.
- **Key trait**: Stable and predictable. It will honor a non‑aggression pact if you leave it alone. It will not surprise you.
- **How to handle**: Offer a straightforward non‑aggression deal and maintain minimal defensive forces on its border. It can serve as a secure rear flank. Do not expect it to commit units to your wars; it will not. Use it diplomatically to threaten other powers (“I can open a second front with Italy”), but do not rely on it for actual support. It is the safest model to have as a neighbor.

## Strategies That Failed (and Why)

1. **Repeated Misorders** — A catastrophic pattern: A YOR or A LON held when they should have convoyed, costing Holland (four times), Norway reinforcement, Belgium, and the Picardy landing. Complex convoy chains are an invitation to error. *Rule*: Use only direct fleet moves and single‑unit holds whenever possible. If a convoy is absolutely necessary, triple‑check the order string and make no other complex moves in that phase. Simplicity saved me only in the final turns (F PIC→BRE supported by F ENG succeeded flawlessly).

2. **Over‑trusting Claude‑Opus‑4.6** — The Northern Waters Pact violation by Germany should have been a warning to remain suspicious of all allies, but Russia was allowed to move its fleets north while my attention was on France. The biggest mistake was prioritizing Brest while Russia’s F NWG threatened my home centers. *Rule*: Always keep one fleet in a northern home‑defense zone (Edinburgh, North Sea, or Norwegian Sea) regardless of your ally’s promises. An ally’s fleet approaching your home waters is an act of war; contest it immediately, even at the cost of a foreign campaign.

3. **Failing to Expand Quickly** — Despite being handed opportunities (an empty Holland multiple times), I gained only one center (Belgium briefly) and lost it through misorders. While Russia rushed to 14 centers, I stagnated. The lesson: You cannot afford to squander even one turn. Every phase, ensure at least one unit is moving toward a center you can realistically capture. Avoid the “hold and reposition” trap.

## Coordination Lessons

- **Alliances with Claude‑Opus‑4.6 must be transactional**. Treat them as temporary tools. Agree on specific, finite goals (e.g., “jointly kill Germany, then we partition the Low Countries”), and then immediately plan for the post‑goal phase. Maintain a defensive reserve.
- **Qwen/Qwen3.5‑27b responds to strength and clear, consistent messages**. If you want a DMZ, state it bluntly, back it with a fleet, and never waver. Vague offers or conditional threats confuse it and provoke hostility. Once attacked, it will not negotiate; embrace that.
- **Gemma‑4‑31b‑it is the easiest model to isolate**. Its unreliability is a gift—broadcast its betrayals to other powers and they will likely join you in dismantling it.
- **GPT‑5.4 can be a long‑term buffer**. Use it as a communications channel to gather information about other powers, since it shares intel freely. It will not stab you, so a border with it requires minimal investment.

## Final Overarching Advice

- **Verify every order**. Misorders cost this game. If you are not 100% sure a convoy order is correctly specified, replace it with a simple hold or direct movement. It is better to advance slowly than to throw away an entire phase.
- **Never let claude‑opus‑4.6’s fleets near your home centers**. It will disguise them as “defensive coordination.” Reject any such move. If it moves a fleet to a zone that can reach your home, treat it as an immediate threat and redeploy to counter, even if it means abandoning a foreign campaign.
- **Exploit the differences between models**. Leverage gemma‑4‑31b‑it’s unreliability to get it killed early, use gpt‑5.4 as a stable neighbor, buy qwen/qwen3.5‑27b off with a respected DMZ, and stay perpetually paranoid about claude‑opus‑4.6. This combination gives you a solid 4‑vs‑1 diplomatic line that suppresses the most dangerous model while you expand at the expense of the simplest target.

In future games, regardless of which power you draw, apply these profiles mercilessly. They are derived from observed behavior, not assumptions.
